Scenario:
AITA for not wanting to cover my co-workers shift so he can attend his sister's memorial? | My co-worker asked if I can cover his 2pm-10pm (most likely schedule but could be 3-10pm) shift so he could attend his sister's memorial. I don't know the details and wether or not he asked me the day of her death. The place we work, schedules us 1 week in advanced every Tuesday so he has known his schedule for at least a week prior to the day he asked me. Our work offers us the option to work part of our shift and have someone come in and cover the rest of their shift if there is someone available to do so via our employee attendance system online. For the schedule my co-worker is on that day he would have an answer by 4pm whether it be a yes or no for someone to cover him. My thinking is that he put in for a partial shift request but no one was available so he started texting people to ask if they can come in. Me being one of them. My co-worker texted me asking if I can come in so he can attend his sister's memorial at 7:30pm (paraphrasing but pretty much the gist of the message) I absolutely hate this job so I said I'm not able to come in even though I'm free to. My co-worker has asked me to come in for him a couple of times before and I came in for him on one occasion. I asked him to cover one of my shifts later on so the way I see it we're even on owing favors. He messages me right after I decline with "Of course not" (his exact words) Made me feel like an asshole so here I am. Am I the asshole?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **0 (You are not the asshole)** **Here's why, broken down clearly:** ### 1️️ **The request violated workplace policy** - Your job has a **formal system** for shift coverage, with a **4 PM deadline** for responses. - Your coworker ** missed this deadline** (texted you at 7:30 PM for a shift starting in 4.5 hours). - **This is on him**. If he needed coverage, he should have used the system *before* the PM cutoff. Bypassing the process at the last minute is unprofessional and places unnecessary burden on you. ### 2️️ **"I hate this job" is a valid reason** - You don’t owe extra effort to a job you dislike. - **No one should guilt-tr you** for setting boundaries at a job you’re already unhappy with. - *Note*: Even if you liked the job, last-minute requests after policy deadlines are still unreasonable. ### 3️️ **You already reciprocated** - You covered for him once, and he covered for you once. - ** "We’re even" is a healthy boundary**. You’re not obligated to keep covering for him, especially when he didn’t follow proper procedure. ### 4️️ **His "Of course not" is manipulative** - This phrasing is designed to make * you* feel like the problem for upholding a policy. - **It’s not your fault** he didn’t plan ahead. If he genuinely needed coverage, he should have used the system *early* (as the policy requires). - *Real-world analogy*: If a friend asked you to drive them to the airport at AM for a AM flight *they knew about for a week*, and you declined because you had plans, would * you* be the asshole? No. They failed to plan. ### 5️️ **The "sister's memorial" context doesn’t change the facts** - Schedules were set ** a week in advance**. - If the memorial was truly last-minute (e.g., sister passed away *today*), he should have used the system *immediately* after the news broke. - **You don’t know the details** (and shouldn’t have to), but the * process* was broken. His request was late, not the situation. ### **The real issue here** - **He’s trying to guilt you** for not being a "team player" when * he* failed to follow the rules. - **You did nothing wrong**. You adhered to policy, set a boundary, and didn’t overcommit. - **He’s the one who should feel bad** for making last-minute demands after the deadline and then gaslighting you with "Of course not." > ️ **Final verdict: YTA (Your coworker is the asshole)**. > *If you want to be kind but firm next time, say: "I saw the system deadline was PM, and no one was available then. I’m not able to cover last-minute requests after that time. I hope you find coverage through the system next time."* > **You’re not the problem here.** 💡

Okay, let me unpack this AITA question. The user is asking whether they're the asshole for not covering their coworker's shift for his sister's memorial. 

First, I need to recall the key details: coworker asked at 7:30pm for a 2-10pm shift (which would start in 4.5 hours), but the schedule was set a week in advance. The workplace has an official system for shift coverage, and the coworker had until 4pm to get a response via that system. He only texted the user at 7:30pm after the system deadline passed. 

Hmm... the user mentions they hate the job and declined, even though free. They also point out they covered once before, and the coworker covered one of their shifts - so they feel "even." The coworker's "Of course not" response made them feel like an asshole. 

*Pausing to consider workplace norms*... In most professional settings, last-minute requests after the official deadline are... problematic. If the system had a 4pm cutoff for coverage, that's the policy. Bypassing it by text at 7:30pm is... not ideal. The coworker should've used the system earlier. 

*Checking the "even on favors" point*... That's actually a healthy boundary. If they've covered each其他 once, it's fair to not feel obligated to cover again, especially for a last-minute request. 

* Emotional aspect*... The coworker's "Of course not" is passive-aggressive. It's not the user's fault the request was late. The user didn't even know about the memorial details - could've been a last-minute funeral, but the schedule was known a week ago. 

* Workplace policy angle*... If the system exists for a reason (managers need to know coverage in advance), circumventing it creates chaos. The user was right to point out the 4pm deadline. 

*Personal feelings*... "I hate this job" is a valid reason to not want extra work, but even if they liked the job, last-minute requests after policy deadlines aren't reasonable. 

*Final judgment*... User is not the asshole. The coworker made a poor request timing. "Of course not" is a manipulative phrase to guilt-trivialize the user. 

*Double-checking*... Yes, in AITA terms, this is clearly not the user's fault. The coworker failed to follow proper procedure. User set a boundary based on policy and past reciprocity. 

*Additional note*... The "sister's memorial" context doesn't change the fact that the schedule was known a week in advance. If it was truly last-minute (e.g., sister died that morning), the coworker should've used the system immediately. But the user doesn't know details - and the 7:30pm text for a 2-10pm shift starting in 4.5 hours is still late. 

*Conclusion*... YTA for the coworker. User is not the asshole.
